title: Faith and reason (CCC 159)
hookLine: truth can't contradict truth; faith and reason are two wings

lines: A PRIEST AND THE BIG BANG.
cards: There's a story a lot of people absorb without anyone telling it to them directly: you have to pick. Science or faith. Reason or religion.
Smart people in labs, pious people in pews, and never the two shall meet. Then you learn that the man who first proposed what we now call the Big Bang was a Belgian Catholic priest.
That the father of genetics was a friar growing peas in a monastery garden. And that the Vatican runs an astronomical observatory. Maybe the story is wrong.

teach.b: First, the claim. Paragraph 159 of the Catechism says that although faith goes beyond reason, there can never be a real conflict between them. Why?

Because the same God who reveals the mysteries of faith also gave human beings the light of reason, and God can't contradict himself. It borrows a line from the First Vatican Council: truth can't contradict truth.

And it adds that honest scientific research, done well and ethically, will never truly conflict with faith, because the things of the world and the things of faith come from the same God. Second, the old root.

teach.h: READ BY THE THINGS THAT ARE MADE.
teach.b: Paul says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made."
To study creation carefully is, for Catholics, one way of reading God's handwriting. Third, the people.

Georges Lemaître, a priest and physicist, proposed in the 1920s and 30s that the universe began from a single primeval atom. Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, worked out the basic laws of heredity.
And honesty matters here: the Church also got it badly wrong with Galileo, condemning him in 1633. In 1992, Pope John Paul II publicly acknowledged the errors of the theologians who judged him.

teach.h: THE INVISIBLE THINGS OF HIM ARE CLEARLY SEEN.
teach.b: In 1998, John Paul II wrote a letter called Faith and Reason. It opens with an image: faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises toward the truth. A bird with one wing just goes in circles.
Catholics are asked to fly with both.

how: Catholic schools and universities teach science alongside theology, the Vatican runs an astronomical observatory, and the Pontifical Academy of Sciences brings together scientists of many faiths and none.

o: an atheist theory meant to disprove creation
a theory first put forward by Albert Einstein
the universe's beginning, first proposed by a priest

p: no real conflict between faith and reason
friar who found the laws of heredity

s: the Catholic Church teaches that faith and science must conflict
the Catechism says there can never be a real conflict, because truth can't contradict truth.
the idea of the Big Bang was first proposed by a Catholic priest
Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist.
the Church has never admitted any error about Galileo
in 1992 John Paul II acknowledged the errors of the theologians who judged him.

games.q: a scientific discovery seems to clash with how you've always understood a Bible passage. what does the Catechism's teaching suggest?
o: keep thinking: truth can't contradict truth, so look more deeply at both
games.why: CCC 159: since the same God gives faith and reason, an apparent conflict is a reason to look more deeply, not to pick a side.

practice: Think of one thing science has taught you that still amazes you: the light from some stars left them before humans existed; your body replaces most of its cells over time; there are more cells in you than stars in our galaxy.
Pick one and let it sink in, with no rush to a lesson, just amazement. If you pray, you can let the wonder turn into thanks.

wordCard.voice: Big Bang, the theory first proposed by a Catholic priest, Georges Lemaître, one of the Church's own examples of faith and reason as two wings. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: faith and reason, the title of John Paul II's 1998 encyclical.

carryVoice: Your line: two wings. Faith and reason, flying together. That's day two hundred ninety-two.
